holding_summary: The court upheld as valid exercises of the police power a municipal ordinance requiring sprinkler systems in non-fireproof rooming houses and an ordinance requiring two means of egress in multi-story rooming houses, rejecting defendants' claims of a protected nonconforming use and confiscatory hardship. The court found no triable fact issues and adjudged defendants guilty on all four counts of violating the Long Beach Municipal Code provisions governing rooming houses.

quotes.text: The Court believes also that the statute here under consideration represents a valid exercise of the City’s police powers and of its inherent right and obligation to protect the health, safety and welfare of its citizens.

In conclusion the court finds that the two ordinances here challenged represent valid and reasonable exercises of the legislative function with which this court has neither the right nor the desire to interfere.

notes: Case concerns municipal safety-code enforcement (sprinklers, egress) against rooming-house owners/operators; the court never classifies the legal character (lease/license/lodging/innkeeping) of the occupants' arrangements, so characterization is left null.

cite: Dowsey v. Village of Kensington, 257 N.Y. 221
notes: Zoning case invalidating a residential-use restriction (one-family/one-housekeeping-unit) as applied to a particular parcel; concerns exclusion of apartments/business, not compensated lodging or boarding.
Upholds an ordinance restricting door-to-door pamphlet distribution absent householder consent; no bearing on lodging, boarding, or letting of rooms.

cite: United Security Corp. v. Suchman, 307 N.Y. 48
notes: Ordinary apartment-lease/statutory-tenancy dispute after mortgage foreclosure; concerns whether a foreclosed lessee becomes a statutory tenant, not short-term lodging or boarding-house regulation.

cite: Self Service Super Market, Inc. v. Harris, 3 N.Y.2d 615
notes: Commercial store lease/statutory tenancy dispute under the Business Rent Law's 'match lease' provision; no connection to residential lodging or boarding.

holding_summary: The Court of Appeals affirmed a zoning area variance permitting the estate owners to continue renting their accessory 'gatehouse' cottage to paying month-to-month tenants, holding they had shown practical difficulties justifying the variance despite an ordinance limiting accessory buildings to occupancy by servants. A variance for the separate 'guest house,' whose paid rental use began only after the ordinance took effect, was properly denied as a self-imposed hardship.

quotes.text: Petitioners have continued to rent the gatehouse (unfurnished) and receive $145 monthly.
The only practical effect of barring the rental of the gatehouse is to deprive the owners of a beneficial use thereof while forcing them to demolish it or have it remain vacant.

We agree with the Appellate Division that petitioners have demonstrated practical difficulties in the way of carrying out the strict letter of the ordinance, and a variance should be granted in order that the spirit of the ordinance may be observed, public safety and welfare secured and substantial justice done.

notes: Householder (estate owner) letting an accessory dwelling on their own property to paying tenants; court treats the rental use as a legitimate, income-producing incident of ownership warranting zoning relief.

cite: East Brooklyn Savings Bank v. Hickman Realty Corp., 272 A.D. 638
court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
notes: Foreclosure/receiver attornment dispute involving a commercial mirror-and-glass shop tenant; no residential lodging or boarding issue.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
notes: Rent-control subtenant-eviction dispute in a mixed residential/commercial building; concerns statutory-tenant protection for apartment subtenants, not householder lodging or boarding-house regulation.

cite: Axelrod v. 11 West 42nd Street, Inc., 274 A.D. 651
court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
notes: Commercial Rent Law dispute over a business that sublets furnished office/desk space with services; not residential lodging or boarding.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
notes: Administrative dispute over how the State Rent Administrator apportions hotel operating-cost increases between rent-controlled rooms and decontrolled transient space; a rate/price-control apportionment question, not licensing/police-power regulation or the right to let, and does not adjudicate the legal character of the lodging.

cite: Laporte v. City of New Rochelle, 2 A.D.2d 710
court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
notes: Zoning dispute over whether a college dormitory for 60+ students qualifies as a single 'family' housekeeping unit; the dissent analogizes to student boarding, but the majority holding turns on the zoning 'family' definition, not compensated letting or boarding-house regulation.

cite: Vivana Realty Corp. v. Abrams, 5 A.D.2d 466
court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
notes: Rent-control decontrol dispute over whether a landlord's conversion of an apartment house into furnished rooms between 1947-1950 qualifies as creation of 'additional housing accommodations'; purely a rate/decontrol interpretation question, not licensing/police-power regulation or the legal character of the letting.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
notes: Rent-control 'under-occupancy' dispute over whether a live-in maid's room counts as occupied space in a luxury apartment; unrelated to lodging or boarding-house practice.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
notes: Dispute over whether a physician's ground-floor office is a 'store' under the Business Rent Law; no connection to residential lodging or boarding.

cite: In re City of New York, 15 A.D.2d 153
court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
notes: Mass condemnation-award appeal; one parcel (a former hotel converted to single-room-occupancy furnished rooms) is valued using a rooming-house-operator rental formula, but the opinion addresses only just-compensation valuation methodology, not the legal character of lodging or its regulation.

cite: Mobile Home Owners Protective Assoc., Inc. v. Town of Chatham, 33 A.D.2d 78
court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
notes: Upholds a town ordinance restricting placement of house trailers/mobile homes outside licensed trailer camps under the police power; concerns owner-occupied mobile homes, not rented rooms or boarding houses.

cite: Shegda v. Village of Lancaster, 192 Misc. 560
holding_summary: The court held that plaintiffs' proposed use of their property as a convalescent home for recuperating patients did not violate the village's residential zoning ordinance, which expressly permits 'hotels, rooming or boarding houses' as of right, because a convalescent home differs only slightly from an ordinary boarding house even with attendant nursing care. Declaratory and injunctive relief were granted in plaintiffs' favor.

quotes.text: In the subdivision of the Village of Lancaster known as and designated as Zone 1 A ’, or Residence District, no building or premises shall be used and no building shall lie erected, constructed, altered or used for any purpose other than that of one or two family dwelling houses, or multiple or apartment houses; and hotels, rooming or boarding houses, churches, schools, club houses and private garages, green houses, nurseries or other building accessory to such private dwellings.
They differ in a very small degree from ordinary boarders.
I find the plaintiffs are entitled to a declaratory judgment in accordance with this opinion and the injunctive relief is hereby granted.

notes: Zoning ordinance affirmatively lists boarding houses alongside dwellings as a permitted residential use, and the court treats lodging/boarding for hire as an ordinary, non-nuisance use analogous to the plaintiffs' convalescent home.

cite: Jacob Reich, Inc. v. Fordon, 234 A.D. 110
court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
notes: Attornment/foreclosure dispute over liability for rent on an apartment lease; ordinary landlord-tenant doctrine unrelated to lodging or boarding-house regulation.
